claim: Nlgn3 is a unique Nlgn isoform that localizes at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Nlgn3 is a unique Nlgn isoform that localizes at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Baudouin et al., 2012; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Uchigashima et al., 2020) and is consistent with the manuscript's own findings.

claim: Nlgn3 localizes at postsynaptic sites apposing vesicular glutamate transporter 3-expressing (VGT3+) inhibitory terminals in mouse organotypic slice cultures.
source: Here we demonstrate that Nlgn3 localizes at postsynaptic sites apposing vesicular glutamate transporter 3-expressing (VGT3+) inhibitory terminals and regulates VGT3+ inhibitory interneuron-mediated synaptic transmission in mouse organotypic slice cultures.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nlgn3 regulates VGT3+ inhibitory interneuron-mediated synaptic transmission.
source: Here we demonstrate that Nlgn3 localizes at postsynaptic sites apposing vesicular glutamate transporter 3-expressing (VGT3+) inhibitory terminals and regulates VGT3+ inhibitory interneuron-mediated synaptic transmission in mouse organotypic slice cultures.
evidence: This is supported by gain-of-function and loss-of-function electrophysiology experiments shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The αNrxn1+AS4 splice isoform is highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with other interneurons.
source: Gene expression analysis of interneurons revealed that the αNrxn1+AS4 splice isoform is highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons as compared with other interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7C and FISH data in Figure 6.

claim: Postsynaptic Nlgn3 requires presynaptic αNrxn1+AS4 expressed in VGT3+ interneurons to regulate inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: Most importantly, postsynaptic Nlgn3 requires presynaptic αNrxn1+AS4 expressed in VGT3+ interneurons to regulate inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments in Nrxn triple knockout mice shown in Figure 8.

claim: Specific Nlgn–Nrxn signaling generates distinct functional properties at synapses.
source: Our results indicate that specific Nlgn–Nrxn signaling generates distinct functional properties at synapses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective experimental findings showing specificity of αNrxn1+AS4-Nlgn3 interactions at VGT3+ synapses.

claim: Signal intensities for Nlgn3 were considerably high at GABAergic synapses co-labeled with VGT3 or CB1.
source: We found that signal intensities for Nlgn3 were considerably high at GABAergic synapses co-labeled with VGT3 or CB1 (Figure 1B,C, and F) and low or at approximately noise levels at those co-labeled with Pv (Figure 1D and F) or Sst (Figure 1E and F) in the CA1 region.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Signal intensities for Nlgn3 were low or at approximately noise levels at GABAergic synapses co-labeled with Pv or Sst.
source: We found that signal intensities for Nlgn3 were considerably high at GABAergic synapses co-labeled with VGT3 or CB1 (Figure 1B,C, and F) and low or at approximately noise levels at those co-labeled with Pv (Figure 1D and F) or Sst (Figure 1E and F) in the CA1 region.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Nlgn3 is preferentially recruited to Cck+ GABAergic synapses, but not to Pv+ or Sst+ inhibitory synapses.
source: Therefore, these data strongly suggest that Nlgn3 is preferentially recruited to Cck+ GABAergic synapses, but not to Pv+ or Sst+ inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing high Nlgn3 signals at VGT3+ and CB1+ synapses (markers for Cck+ interneurons) but not at Pv+ or Sst+ synapses.

claim: Overexpression of Nlgn3Δ in CA1 pyramidal neurons increases uIPSC amplitude at VGT3+ inhibitory synapses.
source: Importantly, VGT3+ inhibitory interneurons displayed clear potentiation of uIPSCs onto CA1 pyramidal neurons overexpressing Nlgn3Δ (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by triple whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nlgn3Δ overexpression reduced paired-pulse depression at VGT3+ synapses.
source: Paired APs of VGT3+ neurons with short intervals (50 ms) induced paired-pulse depression (PPD) of uIPSCs. Nlgn3Δ displayed reduced PPD compared with untransfected neurons, consistent with previous work (Futai et al., 2007; Shipman et al., 2011; Uchigashima et al., 2020; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Paired-pulse ratio inversely correlates with presynaptic release probability.
source: As PPR inversely correlates with presynaptic release probability, these results suggest that Nlgn3Δ OE can facilitate presynaptic GABA release.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of synaptic physiology.

claim: Nlgn3Δ overexpression can facilitate presynaptic GABA release at VGT3+ synapses.
source: As PPR inversely correlates with presynaptic release probability, these results suggest that Nlgn3Δ OE can facilitate presynaptic GABA release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in paired-pulse depression.

claim: Nlgn3Δ overexpression reduced uIPSCs at Pv+ inhibitory synapses.
source: In contrast, Nlgn3Δ OE reduced uIPSCs in Pv+ inhibitory synaptic transmission, but had no effect on PPR as reported previously (Figure 3A–D; Horn and Nicoll, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3B and a citation to Horn and Nicoll, 2018.

claim: Nlgn3Δ overexpression had no effect on PPR at Pv+ inhibitory synapses.
source: In contrast, Nlgn3Δ OE reduced uIPSCs in Pv+ inhibitory synaptic transmission, but had no effect on PPR as reported previously (Figure 3A–D; Horn and Nicoll, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3C.

claim: Nlgn3Δ overexpression did not alter uIPSCs or PPR mediated by Sst+ interneurons.
source: Lastly, Nlgn3Δ OE did not alter uIPSCs or PPR mediated by Sst+ interneurons (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Nlgn3 modifies inhibitory synaptic function depending on the type of presynaptic interneuron with which it interacts.
source: The above results strongly suggest that Nlgn3 modifies inhibitory synaptic function depending on the type of presynaptic interneuron with which it interacts.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Nlgn3Δ overexpression on VGT3+, Pv+, and Sst+ synapses.

claim: Nlgn3Δ overexpression did not increase synaptic connectivity at VGT3+ synapses.
source: Interestingly, Nlgn3Δ OE did not increase synaptic connectivity (Figure 2E), suggesting that (i) Nlgn3 regulates pre-existing inhibitory inputs on postsynaptic neurons and/or (ii) postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ OE is not sufficient to induce new synapse formation.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nlgn3 regulates pre-existing inhibitory inputs on postsynaptic neurons.
source: Interestingly, Nlgn3Δ OE did not increase synaptic connectivity (Figure 2E), suggesting that (i) Nlgn3 regulates pre-existing inhibitory inputs on postsynaptic neurons and/or (ii) postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ OE is not sufficient to induce new synapse formation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of change in connectivity despite functional changes.

claim: Postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ overexpression is not sufficient to induce new synapse formation.
source: Interestingly, Nlgn3Δ OE did not increase synaptic connectivity (Figure 2E), suggesting that (i) Nlgn3 regulates pre-existing inhibitory inputs on postsynaptic neurons and/or (ii) postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ OE is not sufficient to induce new synapse formation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of change in connectivity despite functional changes.

claim: Nlgn3 knockdown reduces uIPSC amplitudes at VGT3+ inhibitory synapses.
source: Compared with untransfected neurons, shNlgn3#1-transfected neurons displayed reduced uIPSC amplitudes mediated by VGT3+ interneurons (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 4B.

claim: Nlgn3 knockdown did not affect uIPSC amplitudes at Pv+ or Sst+ synapses.
source: In contrast, uIPSC amplitudes were affected in neither Pv+ (Figure 4E–H) nor Sst+ (Figure 4I–L) neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figures 4F and 4J.

claim: Nlgn3 is required for synaptic transmission specifically at VGT3+ GABAergic synapses in an input cell-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Nlgn3 is required for synaptic transmission specifically at VGT3+ GABAergic synapses in an input cell-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific reduction of uIPSCs at VGT3+ but not Pv+ or Sst+ synapses upon Nlgn3 knockdown.

claim: NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP mice displayed reduced uIPSC amplitude compared with wild-type VGT3/RFP mice.
source: NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP mice displayed reduced uIPSC, PPR at 25 ms inter-pulse interval, and connectivity compared with wild-type (WT) VGT3/RFP mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5C.

claim: NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP mice displayed reduced PPR at 25 ms inter-pulse interval compared with wild-type VGT3/RFP mice.
source: NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP mice displayed reduced uIPSC, PPR at 25 ms inter-pulse interval, and connectivity compared with wild-type (WT) VGT3/RFP mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5D.

claim: NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP mice displayed reduced connectivity compared with wild-type VGT3/RFP mice.
source: NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP mice displayed reduced uIPSC, PPR at 25 ms inter-pulse interval, and connectivity compared with wild-type (WT) VGT3/RFP mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5E.

claim: Nrxns in VGT3+ interneurons regulate synaptic transmission without changing intrinsic membrane properties.
source: Intrinsic excitability was comparable between WT and NrxnTKO VGT3+ neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). These results suggest that Nrxns in VGT3+ interneurons regulate synaptic transmission without changing intrinsic membrane properties.
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Presynaptic Nrxns in VGT3+ interneurons are not essential for synaptogenesis.
source: VGT3+ interneurons lacking Nrxns induced synaptic release regardless of Nlgn3Δ gene transfection, indicating that presynaptic Nrxns in VGT3+ interneurons are not essential for synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that synaptic transmission still occurs in NrxnTKO neurons.

claim: No enhancement of uIPSC amplitude was observed in Nlgn3-overexpressed neurons compared with untransfected pyramidal neurons when VGT3+ interneurons lack Nrxns.
source: Importantly, we observed no enhancement of uIPSC amplitude in Nlgn3-overexpressed neurons compared with untransfected pyramidal neurons (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5G.

claim: Presynaptic Nrxn proteins are necessary for regulating inhibitory synaptic transmission through postsynaptic Nlgn3.
source: These results strongly suggest that presynaptic Nrxn proteins are necessary for regulating inhibitory synaptic transmission through postsynaptic Nlgn3.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Nlgn3Δ's effect on synaptic transmission in NrxnTKO neurons.

claim: αNrxn1 and βNrxn3 mRNAs appeared to be enriched in scattered cells within the st. radiatum or pyramidale, where VGT3+ interneurons are dominantly distributed.
source: Importantly, αNrxn1 and βNrxn3 mRNAs appeared to be enriched in scattered cells within the st. radiatum or pyramidale (arrows in Figure 6A–C and G–I), where VGT3+ interneurons are dominantly distributed compared with Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data in Figure 6 and a citation to Pelkey et al., 2017.

claim: Double FISH signals were twice as strong for αNrxn1 and βNrxn3 mRNAs in VGT3+ interneurons than in Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons.
source: Double FISH signals were twice as strong for αNrxn1 and βNrxn3 mRNAs in VGT3+ (Figure 6A,G, and J) interneurons than in Pv+ (Figure 6B,H, and J) and Sst+ (Figure 6C,I, and J) interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of FISH signals shown in Figure 6J.

claim: There were no differences in the signal intensities for the remaining Nrxn isoforms between VGT3+ and other interneurons.
source: In contrast, there were no differences in the signal intensities for the remaining Nrxn isoforms between VGT3+ and other interneurons (Figure 6D–F and J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–P).
evidence: This is supported by FISH quantification data in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1P.

claim: αNrxn1 and βNrxn3 mRNAs are highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ or Sst+ interneurons.
source: These findings suggest that αNrxn1 and βNrxn3 mRNAs are highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ or Sst+ interneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH quantification data.

claim: The expression of Nrxn3 is dominant in VGT3+, Pv+, and Sst+ interneurons.
source: The quantification of Nrxn genes indicates that the expression of Nrxn3 is dominant in these three types of interneurons (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: αNrxn1+AS4 was consistently detected as the sole αNrxn1 gene expressed in VGT3+, Pv+, and Sst+ interneurons.
source: Among Nrxn1 splice isoforms, αNrxn1+AS4 was consistently detected as the sole αNrxn1 gene expressed in the three interneurons and highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: αNrxn1+AS4 is highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons.
source: Among Nrxn1 splice isoforms, αNrxn1+AS4 was consistently detected as the sole αNrxn1 gene expressed in the three interneurons and highly expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: βNrxn2+AS4 was the only confirmed Nrxn2 gene expressed in VGT3+, Pv+, and Sst+ interneurons.
source: βNrxn2+AS4 was the only confirmed Nrxn2 gene expressed in the three interneurons but its expression was much lower than that of Nrxn1 and 3 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: βNrxn2+AS4 expression was much lower than that of Nrxn1 and 3 in VGT3+, Pv+, and Sst+ interneurons.
source: βNrxn2+AS4 was the only confirmed Nrxn2 gene expressed in the three interneurons but its expression was much lower than that of Nrxn1 and 3 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: αNrxn3+AS4 and βNrxn3-AS4 were the two major Nrxn3 genes expressed in VGT3+, Pv+, and Sst+ interneurons.
source: αNrxn3+AS4 and βNrxn3-AS4 were the two major Nrxn3 genes expressed in the three interneurons, and αNrxn3+AS4 expression was highest in VGT3+ interneurons compared with other interneurons (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: αNrxn3+AS4 expression was highest in VGT3+ interneurons compared with other interneurons.
source: αNrxn3+AS4 and βNrxn3-AS4 were the two major Nrxn3 genes expressed in the three interneurons, and αNrxn3+AS4 expression was highest in VGT3+ interneurons compared with other interneurons (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: αNrxn1+AS4, αNrxn3+AS4, and βNrxn3-AS4 are the unique Nrxn genes expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons.
source: Therefore, αNrxn1+AS4, αNrxn3+AS4, and βNrxn3-AS4 are the unique Nrxn genes expressed in VGT3+ interneurons compared with Pv+ and Sst+ interneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined FISH and RNA-seq data showing higher expression of these isoforms in VGT3+ interneurons.

claim: Cell pairs overexpressing αNrxn1+AS4 and Nlgn3Δ in presynaptic VGT3/RFP and postsynaptic pyramidal neurons, respectively, displayed significant enhancement of uIPSC with 100% connectivity.
source: Cell pairs overexpressing αNrxn1+AS4 and Nlgn3Δ in presynaptic VGT3/RFP and postsynaptic pyramidal neurons, respectively, displayed significant enhancement of uIPSC with 100% connectivity (Figure 8B,C, and E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figures 8C and 8E.

claim: Presynaptic αNrxn1-AS4 and postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ neuron pairs showed no enhancement of uIPSC compared with control cell pairs.
source: In contrast, presynaptic αNrxn1-AS4/tag-BFP and postsynaptic GFP/Nlgn3Δ neuron pairs showed no enhancement of uIPSC compared with control cell pairs, suggesting that Nlgn3Δ specifically couples with αNrxn1+AS4 to regulate inhibitory synaptic function at VGT3+ synapses.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 8C.

claim: Nlgn3Δ specifically couples with αNrxn1+AS4 to regulate inhibitory synaptic function at VGT3+ synapses.
source: In contrast, presynaptic αNrxn1-AS4/tag-BFP and postsynaptic GFP/Nlgn3Δ neuron pairs showed no enhancement of uIPSC compared with control cell pairs, suggesting that Nlgn3Δ specifically couples with αNrxn1+AS4 to regulate inhibitory synaptic function at VGT3+ synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of αNrxn1+AS4 versus αNrxn1-AS4 on synaptic transmission when paired with Nlgn3Δ.

claim: Neither βNrxn3+AS4 nor βNrxn3-AS4 transfection showed detectable changes in uIPSCs compared with untransfected VGT3/RFP neurons.
source: In contrast with αNrxn1–Nlgn3Δ signals, neither βNrxn3+AS4 nor βNrxn3-AS4 transfection showed detectable changes in uIPSCs compared with untransfected VGT3/RFP neurons, indicating that βNrxn3 is not important for Nlgn3-mediated inhibitory synaptic function.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9B.

claim: βNrxn3 is not important for Nlgn3-mediated inhibitory synaptic function.
source: In contrast with αNrxn1–Nlgn3Δ signals, neither βNrxn3+AS4 nor βNrxn3-AS4 transfection showed detectable changes in uIPSCs compared with untransfected VGT3/RFP neurons, indicating that βNrxn3 is not important for Nlgn3-mediated inhibitory synaptic function.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of βNrxn3 isoforms on synaptic transmission.

claim: βNrxn3-AS4 expressed in NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP/tag-BFP neurons demonstrated reduced connectivity.
source: Interestingly, βNrxn3-AS4 expressed in NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP/tag-BFP neurons demonstrated reduced connectivity (Figure 9D), suggesting that βNrxn3-AS4 protein hinders synapse formation between VGT3/RFP terminals and postsynaptic CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity measurements shown in Figure 9D.

claim: βNrxn3-AS4 protein hinders synapse formation between VGT3/RFP terminals and postsynaptic CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, βNrxn3-AS4 expressed in NrxnTKO/VGT3/RFP/tag-BFP neurons demonstrated reduced connectivity (Figure 9D), suggesting that βNrxn3-AS4 protein hinders synapse formation between VGT3/RFP terminals and postsynaptic CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed reduction in connectivity.

claim: Neither αNrxn3+AS4 nor αNrxn3-AS4 pairing with postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ had any effect on inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: To our surprise, neither αNrxn3+AS4 nor αNrxn3-AS4 pairing with postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ had any effect on inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9F.

claim: αNrxn1+AS4, but not αNrxn3+AS4, has a unique signal in the extracellular domain important for synaptic function with Nlgn3Δ.
source: These results strongly suggest that αNrxn1+AS4, but not αNrxn3+AS4, has a unique signal in the extracellular domain important for synaptic function with Nlgn3Δ.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of αNrxn1+AS4 versus αNrxn3+AS4 on synaptic transmission when paired with Nlgn3Δ.

claim: Trans-synaptic interactions are important for synapse identity, function, plasticity, and maintenance.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that trans-synaptic interactions are also important for synapse identity, function, plasticity, and maintenance (Biederer et al., 2017; Campbell and Tyagarajan, 2019; Südhof, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent review articles.

claim: Four neuroligin genes encode postsynaptic CAMs that contain extracellular cholinesterase-like domains and transmembrane and PDZ-binding motif-containing intracellular domains.
source: Four neuroligin (Nlgn) genes (Nlgn1, Nlgn2, Nlgn3, and Nlgn4) encode postsynaptic CAMs (Nlgn1, Nlgn2, Nlgn3, and Nlgn4) that contain extracellular cholinesterase-like domains and transmembrane and PDZ-binding motif-containing intracellular domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroligin structure.

claim: Each Nlgn protein has a distinct pattern of subcellular localization at excitatory, inhibitory, dopaminergic, and cholinergic synapses.
source: Each Nlgn protein has a distinct pattern of subcellular localization at excitatory, inhibitory, dopaminergic, and cholinergic synapses (Song et al., 1999; Takács et al., 2013; Uchigashima et al., 2016; Varoqueaux et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nlgn3 regulates synaptic functions at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Interestingly, Nlgn3 is the only Nlgn isoform localized at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Baudouin et al., 2012; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Uchigashima et al., 2020), regulating their synaptic functions (Etherton et al., 2011; Földy et al., 2013; Horn and Nicoll, 2018; Shipman et al., 2011; Tabuchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Neurexins are presynaptic CAMs produced from three genes that are transcribed from different promoters as longer alpha, shorter beta, and Nrxn1-specific gamma isoforms.
source: Neurexins (Nrxns) are presynaptic CAMs produced from three genes (Nrxn1, Nrxn2, and Nrxn3) that are transcribed from different promoters as longer alpha (αNrxn1–3), shorter beta (βNrxn1–3), and Nrxn1-specific gamma (γNrxn1) isoforms (Sterky et al., 2017; Tabuchi and Südhof, 2002), and serve as the sole presynaptic binding partners for Nlgns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurexin structure supported by citations.

claim: Neurexins serve as the sole presynaptic binding partners for Nlgns.
source: Neurexins (Nrxns) are presynaptic CAMs produced from three genes (Nrxn1, Nrxn2, and Nrxn3) that are transcribed from different promoters as longer alpha (αNrxn1–3), shorter beta (βNrxn1–3), and Nrxn1-specific gamma (γNrxn1) isoforms (Sterky et al., 2017; Tabuchi and Südhof, 2002), and serve as the sole presynaptic binding partners for Nlgns.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Each Nrxn gene has six alternative splicing sites, named AS1–AS6, resulting in thousands of potential Nrxn splice isoforms.
source: Each Nrxn gene has six alternative splicing sites, named AS1–AS6, resulting in thousands of potential Nrxn splice isoforms (Górecki et al., 1999; Missler et al., 1998; Püschel and Betz, 1995; Schreiner et al., 2014; Treutlein et al., 2014; Ullrich et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Unique transcription patterns of Nrxns have been observed in hippocampal interneurons.
source: Unique transcription patterns of Nrxns have been observed in hippocampal interneurons, suggesting that Nrxn proteins may determine the properties of GABAergic synapses in an input cell-dependent manner (Fuccillo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fuccillo et al., 2015.

claim: Nrxn proteins may determine the properties of GABAergic synapses in an input cell-dependent manner.
source: Unique transcription patterns of Nrxns have been observed in hippocampal interneurons, suggesting that Nrxn proteins may determine the properties of GABAergic synapses in an input cell-dependent manner (Fuccillo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on observed transcription patterns, supported by a citation.

claim: Nrxn–Nlgn interactions depend on Nrxn protein length, splice insertions at AS4 of Nrxns, and splice insertions of Nlgns.
source: Nrxn–Nlgn interactions depend on Nrxn protein length (long form [α] vs short form [β]), splice insertions at AS4 of Nrxns, and splice insertions of Nlgns.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nlgn1 splice variants that have splice insertions at site B have higher binding affinities for βNrxn1-AS4 than for βNrxn1+AS4.
source: For example, Nlgn1 splice variants that have splice insertions at site B have higher binding affinities for βNrxn1-AS4 (βNrxn1 lacking alternative splice insertion at AS4) than for βNrxn1+AS4 (containing an alternative splice insertion at AS4) (Boucard et al., 2005; Koehnke et al., 2010; Reissner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: Nlgn3Δ, which lacks both of the A1 and A2 alternative splice insertions, is the major Nlgn3 splice isoform expressed in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We recently found that Nlgn3Δ, which lacks both of the A1 and A2 alternative splice insertions, is the major Nlgn3 splice isoform expressed in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons and regulates both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission (Uchigashima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: Nlgn3Δ regulates both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We recently found that Nlgn3Δ, which lacks both of the A1 and A2 alternative splice insertions, is the major Nlgn3 splice isoform expressed in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons and regulates both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission (Uchigashima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: There are over 20 classes of inhibitory interneurons in the CA1 area based on molecular markers, action potential firing patterns, and morphology.
source: Indeed, there are over 20 classes of inhibitory interneurons in the CA1 area based on molecular markers, action potential (AP) firing patterns, and morphology (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Interneurons expressing parvalbumin, somatostatin, and cholecystokinin display different morphologies, excitability, and synaptic functions.
source: Among them, interneurons expressing parvalbumin (Pv+), somatostatin (Sst+), and cholecystokinin (Cck+) display different morphologies, excitability, and synaptic functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The trans-synaptic interaction between αNrxn1+AS4 and Nlgn3 underlies the input cell-dependent control of VGT3+ GABAergic synapses in the hippocampus.
source: These results suggest that the trans-synaptic interaction between αNrxn1+AS4 and Nlgn3 underlies the input cell-dependent control of VGT3+ GABAergic synapses in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nlgn2 KO mouse line displays deficits in fast-spiking but not Sst+ interneuron-mediated inhibitory synaptic transmission in the somatosensory cortex.
source: For example, a Nlgn2 KO mouse line displays deficits in fast-spiking but not Sst+ interneuron-mediated inhibitory synaptic transmission in the somatosensory cortex (Gibson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gibson et al., 2009.

claim: Nlgn3 KO mice and the Nlgn3 R451C knock-in mutant line showed Pv+ or Cck+ input-specific abnormal inhibitory synaptic transmission in the hippocampal CA1 region.
source: Furthermore, Nlgn3 KO mice and the Nlgn3 R451C knock-in mutant line, which mimics a human autism mutation, showed Pv+ or Cck+ input-specific abnormal inhibitory synaptic transmission in the hippocampal CA1 region (Földy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Földy et al., 2013.

claim: The function of postsynaptic Nlgns is determined by the type of presynaptic inputs it receives.
source: Therefore, the function of postsynaptic Nlgns is determined by the type of presynaptic inputs it receives, supporting the intriguing hypothesis that specific Nrxn–Nlgn binding regulates synaptic function.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing input-specific effects of Nlgns.

claim: Specific Nrxn–Nlgn binding regulates synaptic function.
source: Therefore, the function of postsynaptic Nlgns is determined by the type of presynaptic inputs it receives, supporting the intriguing hypothesis that specific Nrxn–Nlgn binding regulates synaptic function.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the cited literature and the current study's findings.

claim: Any Nrxn can bind to any Nlgn with different affinities, with the exception of αNrxn1 and Nlgn1, which do not interact.
source: Biochemical studies have demonstrated that any Nrxn can bind to any Nlgn with different affinities, with the exception of αNrxn1 and Nlgn1, which do not interact (Boucard et al., 2005; Reissner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from biochemical studies, supported by citations.

claim: The AS4 insertion has a critical role in changing Nrxns' affinity to postsynaptic binding partners, including Nlgn.
source: The AS4 insertion has a critical role in changing Nrxns' affinity to postsynaptic binding partners, including Nlgn (Südhof, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A splice insertion at AS4 in βNrxn1 can weaken its interaction with Nlgns.
source: A splice insertion at AS4 in βNrxn1 can weaken its interaction with Nlgns (Koehnke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koehnke et al., 2010.

claim: βNrxn1-AS4 but not βNrxn1+AS4 increases synaptic transmission through its interaction with Nlgn1.
source: Indeed, we have reported that βNrxn1-AS4 but not βNrxn1+AS4 increases synaptic transmission through its interaction with Nlgn1 (Futai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: αNrxn1-AS4 specifically interacts with Nlgn2 and enhances inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: Similarly, αNrxn1-AS4 specifically interacts with Nlgn2 and enhances inhibitory synaptic transmission (Futai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: An insertion at AS4 in αNrxn1 can increase inhibitory synaptic transmission at VGT3+ synapses through a trans-synaptic interaction with Nlgn3Δ.
source: In contrast, we found that an insertion at AS4 in αNrxn1 can increase inhibitory synaptic transmission at VGT3+ synapses through a trans-synaptic interaction with Nlgn3Δ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue experiments in Figure 8.

claim: Structural differences beyond the AS4 site exist between αNrxn1 and αNrxn3.
source: It is particularly interesting that only αNrxn1+AS4, but not αNrxn3+AS4, encoded uIPSC enhancement with postsynaptic Nlgn3Δ (Figures 8C and 9F). These results suggest that structural differences beyond the AS4 site exist between these two αNrxns.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential functional effects of αNrxn1+AS4 versus αNrxn3+AS4.

claim: Differential alternative splicing events that occur at other AS sites may regulate binding with Nlgn3Δ.
source: Since the structures of the major Nrxn domains, such as LNS and EGFA-EGFC, are similar between αNrxns, differential alternative splicing events that occur at other AS sites may regulate binding with Nlgn3Δ.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed functional differences between αNrxn1 and αNrxn3.

claim: Nlgns function as homomeric or heteromeric dimers that bind to monomeric Nrxns.
source: Nlgns function as homomeric or heteromeric dimers that bind to monomeric Nrxns (Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Poulopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The function of human Nlgn3A2 at inhibitory synapses requires the presence of Nlgn2 in hippocampal neurons.
source: The function of human Nlgn3A2 at inhibitory synapses requires the presence of Nlgn2 in hippocampal neurons (Nguyen et al., 2016), suggesting that heterodimers of Nlgn3A2 and Nlgn2 are formed at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2016.

claim: Heterodimers of Nlgn3A2 and Nlgn2 are formed at inhibitory synapses.
source: The function of human Nlgn3A2 at inhibitory synapses requires the presence of Nlgn2 in hippocampal neurons (Nguyen et al., 2016), suggesting that heterodimers of Nlgn3A2 and Nlgn2 are formed at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited study.

claim: Deletion of Nrxns or Nlgns has little effect on synapse formation.
source: Deletion of Nrxns or Nlgns has been reported to have little effect on synapse formation (Chanda et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Varoqueaux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trans-synaptic interactions of Nrxns and Nlgns may control not only synapse function but also synapse number.
source: However, Nlgn3Δ formed new synapses only when αNrxn1+AS4 was simultaneously expressed in VGT3+ interneurons (Figure 8E). This suggests that trans-synaptic interactions of Nrxns and Nlgns may control not only synapse function but also synapse number, while the lack of Nrxns or Nlgns on either side of the synapse can be compensated by other CAM interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that connectivity increased only when both αNrxn1+AS4 and Nlgn3Δ were overexpressed.

claim: The lack of Nrxns or Nlgns on either side of the synapse can be compensated by other CAM interactions.
source: However, Nlgn3Δ formed new synapses only when αNrxn1+AS4 was simultaneously expressed in VGT3+ interneurons (Figure 8E). This suggests that trans-synaptic interactions of Nrxns and Nlgns may control not only synapse function but also synapse number, while the lack of Nrxns or Nlgns on either side of the synapse can be compensated by other CAM interactions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the literature showing minimal effects of Nrxn/Nlgn deletion on synapse formation.

claim: Mouse Nlgn3A2 did not potentiate VGT3+ and Sst+ inhibitory synapses.
source: To our surprise, mouse Nlgn3A2 did not potentiate VGT3+ and Sst+ inhibitory synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nlgn3A2 overexpression reduced uIPSCs at Pv+ synapses, like Nlgn3Δ.
source: Nlgn3A2 OE reduced uIPSCs at Pv+ synapses, like Nlgn3Δ (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Nlgn3A2 regulates inhibitory synapses through different interneuron type(s) than Nlgn3Δ.
source: These findings suggest that Nlgn3A2 regulates inhibitory synapses through different interneuron type(s).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Nlgn3A2 versus Nlgn3Δ on different interneuron types.

claim: Pv-Cre and Sst-Cre lines exhibit highly specific cre expression in these cell types, but have leaky cre expression in other cell type(s).
source: However, our current and previous studies for mouse line validation indicate that while Pv-Cre and Sst-Cre lines exhibit highly specific cre expression in these cell types, these lines have leaky cre expression in other cell type(s) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, yellow arrow heads) (Mao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Mao et al., 2015.

claim: Light-evoked activation of nonspecific cell types may contribute to inconsistent results in synaptic transmission measurements.
source: Therefore, light-evoked activation of nonspecific cell types may contribute to the inconsistent results in synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed leaky cre expression.

claim: Cck- and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP)-positive but VGT3-negative inhibitory interneurons have been identified in the hippocampal CA1 region.
source: One possible explanation is that Nlgn3A2 couples with Cck+ neurons that do not express VGT3. Cck- and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP)-positive but VGT3-negative inhibitory interneurons have been identified in the hippocampal CA1 region (Somogyi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Somogyi et al., 2004.

claim: Most of the Cck+ neurons in the hippocampal CA1 area express CB1 transcripts.
source: Furthermore, most of the Cck+ neurons in this area express CB1 transcripts (Katona et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Katona et al., 1999.

claim: CB1 signals can originate from Cck+/VGT3+ and Cck+/VIP+ interneurons.
source: Therefore, CB1 signals in Figure 1C can originate from Cck+/VGT3+ and Cck+/VIP+ interneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on Cck+ neuron subtypes.

claim: Mutations and deletions in Nrxn loci are associated with neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Mutations and deletions in Nrxn loci are associated with neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Copy number alterations and deleterious mutations in αNrxn1 are the most commonly reported Nrxn isoform-specific modifications predisposing people to epilepsy, autism spectrum disorders, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, intellectual disability, schizophrenia, and Tourette syndrome.
source: Copy number alterations (Sebat et al., 2007; Szatmari et al., 2007) and deleterious (Yan et al., 2008; Zahir et al., 2008) mutations in αNrxn1 are the most commonly reported Nrxn isoform-specific modifications predisposing people to epilepsy, autism spectrum disorders (ASDs), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, intellectual disability (ID), schizophrenia (SCZ), and Tourette syndrome (Ching et al., 2010; Clarke et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2008; Møller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Rare mutations in Nlgn3 have been reported in patients with intellectual disability, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorders.
source: Rare mutations in Nlgn3 have been reported in patients with ID, SCZ, and ASDs (Jamain et al., 2003; Parente et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: ASD patients show abnormalities in memory discrimination.
source: Interestingly, ASD patients show abnormalities in memory discrimination (Beversdorf et al., 2000), which is partly mediated by the activity of hippocampal Cck+ interneurons (Sun et al., 2020; Whissell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and preclinical studies.

claim: Memory discrimination is partly mediated by the activity of hippocampal Cck+ interneurons.
source: Interestingly, ASD patients show abnormalities in memory discrimination (Beversdorf et al., 2000), which is partly mediated by the activity of hippocampal Cck+ interneurons (Sun et al., 2020; Whissell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Abnormal memory discrimination in autism may be caused by abnormal trans-synaptic interactions of αNrxn1 and Nlgn3 at VGT3+ synapses.
source: This autistic phenotype may be caused by abnormal trans-synaptic interactions of αNrxn1 and Nlgn3 at VGT3+ synapses.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and cited literature on autism.

claim: Both Nrxn1 and Nlgn3 are expressed at other synapses, including excitatory synapses.
source: In addition to our findings here, both Nrxn1 and Nlgn3 are expressed at other synapses, including excitatory synapses (Baudouin et al., 2012; Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Uchigashima et al., 2019; Uchigashima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
